text:
Collaborative learning enables students to exchange ideas, solve problems together, and develop communication skills. Artificial intelligence can support group work by organising information, suggesting approaches, and helping students coordinate tasks. However, excessive reliance on AI may reduce genuine interaction and weaken the shared reasoning that makes collaboration educationally valuable.

AI can assist groups during the early stages of a project. Students may use it to brainstorm research questions, identify possible sources, or divide a complex topic into manageable sections. Translation and transcription tools can also improve participation among multilingual students or learners with different communication needs.

In addition, AI may help teachers understand group participation. Digital platforms can record contributions, identify patterns of interaction, and highlight students who may be excluded from discussion. This information can allow teachers to intervene and create more balanced opportunities for participation.

However, collaboration becomes less meaningful when AI performs the central intellectual work. A group may appear productive because it has generated a polished report, even though members have spent little time discussing evidence or resolving disagreements. Students may simply divide AI-generated content into sections instead of constructing a shared understanding.

The use of AI may also create unequal participation. Some students may possess stronger prompting and evaluation skills, allowing them to control the group’s direction. Others may accept AI outputs without questioning them. Teachers should therefore assess both the final result and the quality of collaboration.

Effective group tasks can require students to compare perspectives, justify decisions, document revisions, and explain how AI was used. Such requirements make the learning process more visible.

AI can improve collaborative learning by supporting organisation, accessibility, and idea generation. Nevertheless, it should not replace discussion, negotiation, and collective problem-solving. The purpose of group work is not only to produce an answer but also to learn how to think and work with others.
